Regulation · Security · DevOps

CRA reporting duty from 11 September 2026: 24 hours, 72 hours, 14 days

Since 11 September 2026, manufacturers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities – in three stages and on a fixed clock. What this means for development and DevOps teams.

Serge Zabolotny · 2026-10-27

  • Cyber Resilience Act
  • CRA
  • Sicherheitslücken
  • DevOps
  • Compliance
  • ENISA

What this is about

The Cyber Resilience Act (CRA, Regulation (EU) 2024/2847) sets security requirements for products with digital elements. The first duty to apply is reporting actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents: it applies from 11 September 2026, well ahead of the other requirements. The clock starts when the manufacturer becomes aware of active exploitation – not when everything is clarified.

The three deadlines

StageDeadlineContent
Early warning24 hoursMinimal detail, speed over completeness
Notification72 hoursProduct, description, severity, impact, measures taken or planned
Final report14 daysCVE, CVSS score, root cause, remediation, disclosure status, user notification

Reports go through ENISA’s single reporting platform, which forwards them to the national CSIRTs. Separately, affected users must be informed without undue delay. The source names a ceiling of up to €10 million or 2% of worldwide annual turnover for breaches. For details, such as the deadline for severe incidents, please read the regulation text.

Who is affected?

Manufacturers of products with digital elements are obliged. Importers and distributors do not report to ENISA themselves, but must pass vulnerability information to the manufacturer without delay. As I understand it, a pure web service (SaaS) without an accompanying product is not itself a manufacturer under the CRA; whoever ships software or devices that customers run is more likely to be. That is my reading, not an official statement – when in doubt, check it against the regulation text.

What a development team should prepare

  • A named person and a process: who decides within hours whether something is “actively exploited”, and who sends the early warning?
  • An overview of your dependencies: without a list of the libraries in use (an SBOM), “are we affected?” becomes a search in the dark.
  • Fast, repeatable delivery of fixes: a clean CI/CD pipeline is not a luxury here but the precondition for reporting something fixed after 14 days.
  • A channel to users: how do you reach your customers when an update is urgent?

This fits what I describe in the notes on zero trust for the homelab and on NIS2 for small IT companies: anyone who knows their access paths and dependencies has an advantage under both regimes.

Sources and limits

  • CRA Compliance Hub: Article 14 (secondary source, as of October 2026)
  • Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 in the Official Journal – the binding text

Not legal advice. I am a developer, not a lawyer. The details come from the sources listed (as of October 2026); the legal text is what counts.
